---
title: Estimating how much things change
subtitle: Linear models
---

Picture the lab meeting. You show the GFAP data from the ischemia study, and a labmate asks the question every one of us has been asked: "So, does it go up?" You say yes. Then comes the follow-up that decides whether your analysis was any good: "How much? Per day? And how sure are you?" A test that says the groups differ has nothing to offer here. It answers a question nobody at the bench was really asking. What your labmate wants is a number with an honest margin around it, something like "about this much per day, give or take that much," and a statement about whether the world could plausibly have produced it by chance. @fig-linear-models-intro-dimmer is the picture I keep in mind: a switch against a dimmer.

![A significance test is a light switch: on or off. A model is a dimmer: how bright, and give or take how much.](images/linear-models-intro_switch-and-dimmer.png){#fig-linear-models-intro-dimmer fig-align="center" width="90%" fig-alt="Watercolor sketch of a wall with two fixtures, each with a bare bulb hanging above it. On the left, a rocker light switch with a bulb glowing evenly. On the right, a round dimmer knob set at about two thirds, with a bulb whose glow fades through rings of ochre light into a soft translucent teal band."}

Producing that number is the whole job of this part. In the last part we only looked: we learned what a row is, cleaned the table in a script, asked what a missing value was hiding, and drew every point by group. Now we ask a model to commit. And since the book is meant to be read by people who arrive with a question rather than a technique, I have named the chapters accordingly. From here on, each chapter title says what you are trying to *do* with your data (track tissue loss, count cells, estimate how likely a mouse is to cross a wire), and the technique comes second, as a subtitle. Nobody walks into the lab wanting a negative binomial. People walk in wanting to count cells, and the negative binomial is what turns out to be needed.

## What you'll do in the next five chapters

The arc is a single idea told in five steps: *draw a line, trust it, narrow it to where it holds, ask what else explains it, and decide whether a line was the right model all along*.

**We start by describing a change** (@sec-linear-regression-what). Before any new technique, we stop and ask what the straight line you already fitted in the first part actually *is*: an intercept, a slope, and a leftover. We take the equation apart piece by piece, using the same data, and finish by drawing one line across the whole time course of the ischemia study. I will tell you right away that it looks wrong, and the next chapter is about why.

**Then we check whether the line deserves our trust** (@sec-linear-regression-assumptions). A line is easy to draw and easy to believe. `lm()` and `brm()` will fit one to anything, without a murmur. Here we meet the assumptions behind it, and the first surprise is whose they are: not the equation's, but yours. The two that matter most, whether your data map onto your question and whom they represent, no plot can check. Then we watch several of the others fail on real data: the curve that a straight line cannot follow, and the spread that widens exactly where the injury is worst. We also ask why the habit of running a test for every assumption protects you so little (the evidence is in @sec-appendix-assumption-tests). Everything in the first part of the book that you noticed with your own eyes becomes, in this chapter, something with a name and a check.

**Next we track tissue loss after ischemia** (@sec-linear-regression-single-continuous). Armed with the diagnosis, we restrict ourselves to the stretch of the time course where a straight line is a defensible description, and we estimate how much hemispheric tissue is lost per day, with a Bayesian fit and a frequentist one side by side.

**Then we ask whether anything else explains the loss** (@sec-linear-regression-multiple). GFAP is the star of this dataset, so surely it explains tissue loss. I will show you how that hunch behaves when time is added to the model, and what the word "adjusting" really means once you have watched it eat an association. This is also where we meet interactions and transformations, and where the design of the experiment tells us, politely but firmly, which questions the data cannot answer.

**Finally we decide whether a line was the right model** (@sec-linear-models-reflection). The last chapter of this part has no new technique. We reread the four before it as a sequence of decisions, put the line next to its neighbors answering the same question about the same animals, and ask when a line is enough and when it is not. Nothing in statistics makes it the default; the question is what your question, your outcome and your design need.

That is where this part stops, deliberately, at the edge of what a line can do. What the next part changes is not the logic but the noise: the things we count, score and time at the bench rarely scatter the way a bell curve says they should.

## Three things to know before you start

First, **the data are the ones you already know**. The histology data, `cell_data`, are the same ones you got to know in the last part, and they carry every chapter of this one. When a new dataset arrives later in the book, it comes with a plain account of what one row is and how it was obtained. That habit is the one we built in the last part, and it matters more as the outcomes get less familiar: before you trust a model, you should know what was measured.

Second, **the two lenses stay on**. Every applied model is fitted with `brms` and with its frequentist counterpart, in tabs, and each chapter closes by saying where the two agree and where they part ways.

Third, **one thing is deliberately left for later**. Throughout this part, every row is treated as an independent observation: one row per animal in the histology data. Where a chapter meets structure that isn't independent, it says so and tells you what that costs, and where it isn't ready to repair it yet, it says that too. Those are the cracks that the hierarchical models later in the book are built to seal. I'd rather you meet the problem once you can recognize it than have me hide it.

::: callout-tip
If you have never fitted a regression, the next chapter assumes nothing beyond the Bayesian vocabulary of the first part and the habits of the second. If you have, I'd still read the first two chapters: they fix the words (intercept, slope, residual, assumption) that every later chapter uses without stopping to re-explain.
:::

So let's go back to the question from the lab meeting: not "does it go up?" but *how much, per day, and how sure are we*. On to @sec-linear-regression-what.
